How the borrow checker tracks ownership in Rust

By Ada Example

Every value in a Rust program has exactly one owner at any moment, and the compiler keeps a precise record of who that owner is. When the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, which means memory is released at a point the compiler can name long before the program ever runs.

Borrowing lets other parts of the program look at a value without taking it away from its owner. The compiler accepts any number of shared borrows at the same time, or exactly one exclusive borrow, but it never accepts both together, because that combination is what makes data races possible.

Moves and copies

Assigning a value to a new variable moves it, and the old variable can no longer be used. Small types such as integers opt out of this rule by being copied instead, so both variables stay usable afterwards and nothing surprising happens when one of them changes later on.

A function that takes a value by parameter becomes its new owner for the length of the call. Passing a reference instead keeps ownership with the caller, and the function body is checked to make sure that reference never escapes into a place that lives longer than the value it points to.

Lifetimes

Lifetimes are the names the compiler gives to the regions of code in which a borrow is valid. Most of the time they are inferred, and you only write them out when a function returns a reference and the compiler needs to be told which argument that reference was derived from.

The checker reasons about control flow, so a borrow ends at its last use and not at the closing brace of the block. Code that looks like it holds two conflicting borrows often compiles because the first one is already finished by the time the second one begins. See the lifetimes guide for worked examples.
